title: Three at the table
hookLine: when three eat together, one invites the others to bless

cards: Friday night. The meal is over, plates pushed back, someone still picking at the cake. Then one person clears their throat and says, half singing, in Yiddish or Hebrew: friends, let's bless.
Everyone stops and answers. It's a tiny call and response, maybe fifteen seconds long, and it only happens when at least three people ate together. Two people bless on their own.

teach.b: It's called zimmun, an invitation, from a root that means to call together. The Mishnah in Berakhot rules that three who ate together are obligated to make it.
The Talmud finds the source in a psalm: "O magnify the LORD with me, and let us exalt His name together." One person invites, the others join. In many homes it goes like this.
The leader says: friends, let us bless, in Hebrew rabbotai nevarech, or in the old Yiddish, rabbosai, mir vellen bentshen.
Everyone answers with a verse from Psalm 113: "Blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and for ever." The leader repeats it, then says: let us bless the One whose food we have eaten.
The table answers: blessed is the One whose food we have eaten, and through whose goodness we live. Then the grace continues.
With ten people, God's name, Eloheinu, our God, is added to the invitation. The Talmud also says that women may form a zimmun of their own.
In some communities today, men and women together, or women leading, are welcomed; in others, practice stays more traditional. Each community follows its own teachers.

What's striking is the shape. Someone has to ask the others to join, and they have to say yes out loud. A meal shared becomes thanks shared, and for a minute the table turns into a small congregation.

how: When three or more Jewish adults eat bread together, one leads the zimmun, the invitation to grace, and the others respond before Birkat HaMazon; with ten, the word Eloheinu is added. Who may lead and join varies between communities.

games.why: one calls, friends, let us bless, and the others answer out loud: the zimmun.

practice: Picture the next meal you'll share with at least two other people and the moment it ends: imagine being the one who says, before we get up, let's say thank you, and hearing them answer.
If you pray, you can picture the zimmun itself, or the psalm's let us exalt His name together; if not, a simple let's thank whoever made this will do. Then sit for a while with who's at that table.
